product.title: Indonesian 101 new edition
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you into Bahasa Indonesia from absolute zero: short dialogues from real Indonesian life, word-for-word translations that show you how the language actually assembles a sentence, compact grammar notes, full vocabulary with pronunciation, exercises, and an answer key. Written in English for learners who do not speak Indonesian yet, and it teaches the Indonesian that people really speak — the formal sentence and the everyday one side by side, because in Indonesia you will hear both on the same day.

blocks.text: Indonesian is the easiest major language in the world to start, and one of the hardest to be told the truth about. Most books either flatter you — "no tenses, no plurals, you'll be fluent in a month!" — or bury you in a system of prefixes and suffixes that no beginner needs on day one. This book does neither.

Here is the honest version. Indonesian gives you four extraordinary gifts, and they are real. **Verbs never change.** *Makan* is "eat", and it stays *makan* for I, you, he, she, we, they — yesterday, today and tomorrow. **There is no verb "to be" in the present.** *Saya guru* is a complete, correct sentence: "I (am a) teacher." **There is no grammatical gender and there are no articles** — no *le/la*, no *der/die/das*, no *a/the* to agonise over. And **the spelling is phonetic**: what you see is what you say, in the Latin alphabet you already own.

That is not marketing. It means that by the end of Unit 1 you will be making real sentences, and by Unit 5 you will be talking about the past and the future without having learned a single verb ending.
Now the part the brochures leave out. Indonesian has three genuine difficulties, and this book meets all three head-on instead of hiding them until Book Two.

items: **Pronouns are a politeness system, not a word list.** English has one "you". Indonesian makes you choose between *kamu*, *Anda*, *Bapak*, *Ibu*, *Mas*, *Mbak* and simply using the person's name — and the wrong choice sounds either cold or rude. Unit 3 is devoted to it.

**Affixes.** *Beli* means "buy"; *membeli*, *dibeli*, *pembeli*, *pembelian* and *belian* are all built on it. You do not need to produce these at A1, but you must be able to see the root inside the word. This book teaches you to strip the word down, and introduces only the affixes you will actually use.

**There are two Indonesians.** The one on the news and in this book's formal sentences, and the one people speak in the street — *nggak* for *tidak*, *udah* for *sudah*, *gimana* for *bagaimana*. Learn only the first and you will not understand a taxi driver. Learn only the second and you cannot write an email. Every unit here gives you both, marked clearly.

blocks.text: One more thing about word order, because it will save you weeks. Indonesian questions **do not rearrange the sentence**. *Anda guru.* ("You are a teacher.") becomes *Anda guru?* — the same words, with your voice going up at the end. And the question word can stay exactly where the answer would be: *Anda tinggal di mana?* is literally "You live at where?". Nothing moves. If you are coming from English, this is one habit you get to drop rather than one you have to build.
The explanations in this book are deliberately short. What is long is the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Give this twenty to thirty uninterrupted minutes, not two broken hours. Languages stick through short frequent repetition, not through one long assault.
Read every dialogue **out loud**. Indonesian is spelled the way it sounds, so reading aloud costs you nothing and buys you an accent.
Do not skip the word-for-word line under each sentence. That line is where you actually see how Indonesian thinks — and it is the reason you will stop translating from English by about Unit 8.
Do the exercises before you look at the key. Getting one wrong and finding out why is worth ten sentences read passively.

blocks.text: Every unit has the same shape, and the shape is the method. It comes from the classic European self-study courses — Assimil, Teach Yourself — adapted for a language that has no conjugation to drill.

items: **Dialogue.** Ten to twelve lines of Indonesian people actually saying something to each other. Under each line: the natural English, and then the word-for-word English in small type.
**Notes.** Four or five things in that dialogue that would have quietly confused you.
**Grammar boxes.** One point each, with a table you can photograph and keep.
**Extra sections.** Word fields, useful phrase lists, culture — the things a phrasebook has and a grammar book does not.
**Vocabulary.** Everything new in the unit, with pronunciation and English.
**Exercises and answer key.** Between fifteen and twenty-five items per unit, and the key is right there.

blocks.text: **The word-for-word line is the engine of this book.** When you read *Saya mau makan* and the line under it says "I want eat", you are not being given a clumsy translation — you are being shown that Indonesian stacks two verbs with nothing between them. After twenty units of this, Indonesian sentence patterns stop being rules you memorise and start being shapes you recognise.

**About the wave.** At the end of most units there is a short *wave review* line telling you which earlier unit to re-read today. Ignore it and you will forget Unit 2 by Unit 9. It costs five minutes and it is the single highest-return habit in this book.
**A realistic pace:** one unit every two days, one wave review each time. That is six weeks to the end of the book, and by then you can survive a week in Indonesia on your own.

💬 — the everyday spoken form. What people really say, as opposed to what is written.

blocks.text: Indonesian spelling is almost perfectly phonetic: each letter has one sound, and that sound does not change from word to word. There is exactly **one** ambiguity in the whole system — the letter *e* — and this page tells you how this book handles it.
1. The five vowels
Vowels are short and clean. They never glide the way English vowels do: *o* in *roti* is a single pure "oh", not "ohw".
2. The two e's — and how this book marks them

The letter *e* stands for two different sounds, and Indonesian writing does not distinguish them. *Enak* ("tasty") has the *e* of "bed". *Empat* ("four") has the tiny neutral vowel of "about" — the schwa — and it is by far the more common of the two.

So in the **Say it** column of every vocabulary table in this book, the schwa is written **uh**, and the stressed syllable is written in CAPITALS. Nothing else is respelled, because nothing else needs to be.

When the *e* is the "bed" sound rather than the schwa, this book writes it **É** in the Say it column. When you see plain **uh**, it is the schwa. That is the entire pronunciation notation — there is nothing else to learn.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **The ng at the start of a word.** *Nggak* ("no", the everyday form) begins with a sound English only ever puts at the *end* of a word. Say "sing", hold the final sound, then add "-gak". Indonesians will understand you long before you get it perfect.
⚠️ **Final k is a stop, not a click.** In *tidak*, *enak*, *anak*, the final *k* is swallowed — the throat closes, but no "k" is released. It sounds like the gap in the middle of "uh-oh".
4. Stress

Indonesian stress is light and almost always on the **second-to-last syllable**: *ma-KAN-an*, *se-la-MAT*, *bu-KU*. It carries much less weight than in English — getting it wrong will not make you unintelligible. That is why this book marks it once, in the vocabulary tables, and then stops bothering you about it.
One systematic exception: when the second-to-last syllable contains a schwa, the stress slides onto the last one. *Empat* is **uhm-PAT**, not "UHM-pat"; *belum* is **buh-LUM**.
5. What you can stop worrying about

items: **No tones.** Unlike Thai, Vietnamese or Mandarin, pitch carries no meaning. Say it flat; you will be understood.
**No silent letters.** Every letter you see is pronounced.
**No long/short vowel distinction.** *Bisa* and *bisa* are the same word however long you hold the vowel.
**No consonant clusters at the start of words**, apart from a handful of loanwords. Indonesian syllables are open and easy: *ba-ha-sa*, *ke-lu-ar-ga*.

blocks.text: You have finished twenty units. In CEFR terms you are at a solid **A1**, and closer to A2 in listening than the label suggests, because Indonesian gives you so much for free. Concretely: you can introduce yourself, ask for and understand prices and directions, order food, take a taxi or an ojek, describe your family and your day, talk about what you did yesterday and what you plan to do tomorrow, and get help when something goes wrong.
Where the next real jump is

items: **The me- verbs, actively.** So far you have been recognising them. Learning to build them (*beli → membeli*, *tulis → menulis*, *sapu → menyapu*) is what makes your written Indonesian stop sounding like a text message.
**The passive with *di-*.** Indonesian uses the passive far more than English does — notices, instructions and news are full of it. *Dilarang merokok.* "Smoking is forbidden."
**-kan and -i.** The two suffixes that turn one verb into three. *Buka* (open), *bukakan* (open for someone), *bukai* — this is where B1 begins.

**Listening to unscripted speech.** Indonesian slang, particles and swallowed syllables are a wall until you have had a hundred hours of exposure. Start with anything where people talk to each other rather than to a camera.

blocks.text: How to keep the twenty units alive
Re-read one unit a week, out loud, in a random order. Twenty weeks later start again. This costs ten minutes and it is the difference between a language you once studied and a language you have.

And then use it. Indonesian speakers are, as a rule, delighted and forgiving when a foreigner tries — you will get more encouragement per mistake here than in almost any other language. *Selamat belajar!*
